title: Abhishek Sharma Blazed 59 off 24 Balls. Shreyas Iyer Made 68. Rain Made It All Count for Nothing.
excerpt: India posted 189/7 after being reduced to 6/2, but persistent rain in Durham washed out England's chase and the series opener ended without a result
body:
CHESTER-LE-STREET — For about two hours on a cool Wednesday evening in Durham, India played some of the most exhilarating T20 cricket they have produced in months. Then the sky opened up and none of it mattered.

The first T20I between England and India at the Riverside Ground was abandoned without a result after persistent rain washed out the second innings. India, who had recovered brilliantly from 6 for 2 to post 189 for 7, never got to defend their total. The five-match series remains level at 0-0.

It was the cruellest possible anticlimax for a team that had arrived in England under intense scrutiny after a humiliating 2-0 whitewash in Ireland.

## From Disaster to Dominance

Shreyas Iyer won the toss and chose to bat — a decision that seemed catastrophic within the first two overs. Sanju Samson fell for 1, caught off Saqib Mahmood's seaming delivery, and Ishan Kishan — who had been crowned the world's No. 1 ranked T20I batter just hours earlier — was run out for a two-ball duck after a calamitous mix-up with Abhishek Sharma.

India were 6 for 2 and staring at a repeat of Belfast.

What followed was the fightback the Indian camp desperately needed. Abhishek Sharma and Shreyas Iyer added 82 runs in just 38 deliveries, an explosive partnership that shifted the momentum entirely. Abhishek was the aggressor, taking apart Mahmood's second over for 21 runs — four, six, six in succession — before continuing to dismantle Will Jacks and Liam Dawson with equal contempt.

He raced to his fifty off just 20 balls, his trademark destruction of pace and spin on full display. In the process, he became the fastest batter in history to reach 100 sixes in T20 internationals, getting there in just 785 balls — overtaking West Indian Evin Lewis's record of 789. Sam Curran eventually trapped him LBW for 59 off 24, but the damage was done.

## Iyer Answers His Critics

With questions mounting over his captaincy after the Ireland debacle, Shreyas Iyer let his bat do the talking. He reached his first half-century as T20I captain off 38 balls — becoming the first Indian captain to score a T20I fifty on English soil — and continued to play expansive shots through cover and over the top. He fell to Mahmood for 68 off 47, but not before anchoring India past the 160-run mark.

Tilak Varma contributed a brisk 13 before falling to a Mahmood scoop-shot trap, with Liam Dawson taking a fine catch at short fine leg. That brought Shivam Dube to the crease, and the Mumbai all-rounder provided India with the perfect finish — an unbeaten 42 off 21 balls, crashing two fours and three sixes as rain began spotting the outfield during the final overs.

Saqib Mahmood was England's standout with 3 for 33 in four overs, including the early wicket of Samson. Sam Curran and Adil Rashid picked up a wicket each, with Rashid stumping Harshit Rana, who had been promoted as a lower-order hitter.

## Rain Gets the Final Word

The downpour that had threatened all evening intensified during the innings break and never relented. Ground staff covered the square and waited, but the rain only grew heavier. With overs ticking away, the umpires eventually called the match off.

For India, the frustration is acute. They had done everything right after those disastrous first two overs. For England, the reprieve is welcome — they never had to chase 190 on a surface that had begun to slow up.

## What It Means for the Series

The abandoned match means both teams walk away with nothing. No points, no result, and no clarity on where this series is heading. The second T20I moves to Old Trafford in Manchester on Saturday, July 4, where India will hope for better weather and a chance to convert their batting form into an actual win.

For the thousands of Indian fans who had packed the Riverside Ground — many of whom had travelled from London, Birmingham, and the Midlands for the occasion — the washout was a bitter pill. The NRI community in the UK has long treated India's tours as marquee sporting events, and losing the opener to weather rather than a contest will sting.

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the 18-year-old prodigy whose international debut has become Indian cricket's most anticipated moment, was once again left on the bench. His wait continues.

The series moves to Manchester. India will bring the same intent. They will just need the weather to cooperate.
